General Scheme 
Private Wires Bill 2025 (Amendments to Electricity Regulation Act 1999) 
 
Heads 
1. Long title 
2. Short title 
3. Deﬁnitions 
4. Additional function of the Commission regarding electrical safety 
5. A safety regime for private wires 
6. Licencing of private wires 
7. Insertion of section on private wires 
8. Provision to ensure the reviewing of private wires legislation  
9. A safety regime for internal collector cable systems 
10. Commencement Date for Head 9 
11. Funding of CRU in the development of a Private Wires regime

2 
 
Head 1 – Long title 
Long Title of the Act 
Provide that: 
This Act may be cited as the Private Wires Act 2026, under which the Electricity Regulation Act 1999 
will be amended to provide for private wires whereby private developers will be able to own and 
operate electricity lines in ﬁnite circumstances and to give the Minister for Climate, Energy and the 
Environment and the Commission for Regulation of Utilities powers to regulate, licence and monitor 
the implementation of private wires. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
To provide for the long title of this Act

3 
 
Head 2 – Short title 
To provide that: 
This Act may be cited as the Private Wires Act, 2026. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
To provide for a short title by which the Act may generally be referred.

4 
 
Head 3 - Deﬁnitions 
To provide that Section 2 of the 1999 Act, is amended by the insertion of a ‘private wire’ deﬁnition 
and amendment to the ‘electricity undertaking’ deﬁnition, and the insertion of a ‘internal collector 
cable systems’ deﬁnition: 
‘private wire’ means an electric line owned by a person or entity which is used or is to be used to 
carry electricity for the purpose of supply and the construction of which line is permitted under 
Section 37A or licenced under Section 14.  
‘electricity undertaking’ means any person engaged in generation, transmission, distribution,  
aggregation, demand response, energy storage, supply or purchase of electricity, and who is 
responsible for the commercial, technical or maintenance tasks related to those functions, including 
a holder of a licence or authorisation under the 1999 Act or a person who has been granted a permit 
under Section 37 of the 1927 Act, and participants in the private wires scheme but does not include 
any other ﬁnal customers. 
‘internal collector cable systems’ refer to the collector system of cables used to consolidate the 
power generated by individual units of a single generation project for the purpose of export via a 
single grid connection point.   
 
Explanatory Note: 
To provide for relevant deﬁnitions.  
The deﬁnition of private wires will be inserted into the 1999 Act. The deﬁnition of Private Wires will 
provide for the distinction of this infrastructure from that which makes up a transmission system or a 
distribution system as set out under the deﬁnitions of ‘transmission’ and ‘distribution’ in Section 2 of 
the 1999 Act. The intention is for this deﬁnition to also distinguish private wires from ‘transmission 
system operator’ and ‘distribution system operator’ as deﬁned in the 1999 Act and the Directive 
2019/944 (the Internal Market for Electricity Directive).  
The deﬁnition of electricity undertaking will also be amended in the 1999 Act to clarify that private 
wires fall outside the scope of the deﬁnition of ‘ﬁnal customer.’ This is to allow for private wires to be 
included in the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) Levy Order under Schedule I of the 1999 
Act and to resolve concerns around the issue of supply to ﬁnal customers. 
The deﬁnition of “internal collector cable systems” is introduced in order to provide clarity on 
previously referred to “internal networks” outlined in the approved policy statement. Wind and solar 
farms often have extensive networks of cables to collect generated electricity from individual wind 
turbines or solar panels and bring them to a central point where the farm connects to the national 
grid. These internal systems of collector cables should be appropriately regulated and overseen by the 
CRU as there is currently no publicly adopted standards or mechanisms to inspect such systems. The 
change from “internal networks” to “internal collector cable systems” is made to ensure that the term 
private networks and internal networks are not conﬂated. It is outlined in the policy statement that 
these internal collector cables will be legislated for alongside private wires.

5 
 
Head 4 – Additional function of the Commission regarding electrical safety. 
To provide that Section 9 of the 1999 Act, is amended by the insertion of a Section 9(1)(ee):  
to regulate the activities of holders of private wire licences under section 14(1)(p) of the 1999 Act 
and holders of private wire permissions under Section 37A of the 1999 Act with respect to safety. 
 
 
Explanatory Note:  
This amends the 1999 Act to include the function of regulating private wires as part of the CRU’s role. 
Under the existing legislative framework, ESB Networks have a monopoly on distribution grid 
development and ownership including sole oversight of the electrical safety and technical standards 
to which the grid is built. EirGrid oversees the operation of the national transmission grid. 
Expanding ownership of electricity lines to private developers in the case of private wires requires the 
CRU to assume oversight of the electrical safety of private wires. It is intended that the technical and 
safety management of the national grid – i.e. the transmission and distribution network – will remain 
in the oversight of ESB Networks and EirGrid; the CRU’s role will solely pertain to private wires. 
The reference to a licence under Section 14 is set out in Head 6.

6 
 
Head 5 – A safety regime for Private Wires 
To provide that Section 9C of the 1999 Act, is amended by the insertion of a Section 9CA: 
Where: 
(a) The Commission shall, in consultation with the Minister, make regulations relating to 
electrical safety of private wires. 
(b) The Commission shall consult the Board and EirGrid in preparation of regulations to ensure 
private wires are functionally compliant with the electrical, technical and safety standards of 
the national grid. 
(c) The Commission shall specify procedures regarding the installation, operation, maintenance 
and decommissioning of private wires. 
(d) The Commission shall make regulations to designate procedures for the inspection of private 
wires to evaluate compliance with any regulations made regarding safety standards set by 
the Commission. 
(e) The Commission may appoint a person to act as an electricity safety oﬃcer for the purposes 
of inspecting and enforcing the safety standards of private wires. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
This head provides that the CRU will have the responsibility to set out private wire’s safety standards 
in regulations.  
It includes the requirement that the CRU will consult with ESB Networks and EirGrid regarding 
functional speciﬁcations of private wires. The CRU will also have the power to make regulations around 
the inspection of private wires and compliance with the standards set by the organisation. This should 
also include reference to emergency and incident response particularly in the case of risks to public 
safety. The section speciﬁes that all private wires will be built to the same safety standards as the 
national grid. 
Subsection (e) gives the CRU powers to appoint an electrical safety oﬃcer to enforce the private wires 
safety regime set out in the above regulations. This person may or may not be a member of the CRU 
itself.

7 
 
Head 6 – Licencing of private wires 
To provide that Section 14 of the 1999 Act, is amended by the insertion of a Section 14(1)(p): 
To discharge the functions of a private wire (in line with Head 7) 
 
Explanatory Note: 
It will be required that some developers or private entities seeking to build a private wire will need to 
apply to the CRU for a private wire licence. Head 7 speciﬁes in which cases applications need to be 
made to the CRU for a private wire licence and in which cases a permission for a private wire is 
suﬃcient. For clarity, a private wires licence is a licence to construct a single asset and is not to be 
construed as a private wires operator licence. 
The implication here is that, in some cases, private wires may be transporting large volumes of high 
voltage electricity over signiﬁcant distances, for example, from a wind farm to a large energy user. In 
this case there would be in the public interest to more stringently regulate the safety and technical 
standards of the private wires and to allow for a licence fee for the CRU to recoup the admin costs 
required to evaluate applications. Introducing a private wires licence for these large-scale projects is 
preferable because the existing licence regime under the 1999 Act has provisions of application fees.  
In the case of on street electric vehicle (EV) charging, it is anticipated that a licence will not be required 
to build a small-scale private wire, but rather an authorisation sought from the relevant local authority 
including potentially a road opening licence (as in the case of on-street EV charging that crosses a 
pathway). 
The speciﬁc circumstances that require either a) a licence from CRU or b) a less stringent permissions 
are speciﬁed in Head 7.

8 
 
Head 7 – Insertion of section on Private Wires 
To provide that Section 37 of the 1999 Act, is amended by the insertion of: 
Section 37A – Private Wires 
1. To provide that the Commission can grant or refuse to grant a Private Wires licence to 
construct a private wire not connected to the transmission or distribution systems when 
initially constructed to facilitate the supply of electricity in the following instances: 
a. A new source of generation, or battery storage, connecting directly to a customer or 
another electricity undertaking. 
2. To provide that the Commission can grant or refuse to grant a Private Wires permission to 
construct a private wire not connected to the transmission or distribution systems when 
initially constructed to facilitate the supply of electricity in the following instances: 
a. Where more than one generation technology or electricity storage technology intend 
to share a single grid connection including if there are multiple legal entities 
involved. 
b. To allow a customer self-supplying electricity to generate electricity onsite and 
supply it to a separate customer on a contiguous premises.  
3. To provide local authorities with the powers to authorise the running of electricity lines in 
public or shared spaces to enable electric vehicle charging for domestic premises. Local 
authorities shall notify the Board of the existence of such wires and shall update the 
Commission on new or additional private wires on an annual basis.  
4. The Commission will not grant a licence or permission unless an application suﬃciently 
demonstrates that: 
a. That the private wire will promote the use of renewable, sustainable or alternative 
forms of energy taking into consideration project-level security of supply concerns. 
b. That the private wire will not interfere with the operation of the national grid and 
national security of supply. 
c. That a private wire will not interfere with any planned expansion or reinforcement of 
the national grid. 
5. A licence or a permission to construct a private wire under subsection 1 and subsection 2 of 
this section will require the licence holder or permission holder to comply with safety 
standards that will be set out by the Commission under Section 9CA. 
6. A licence to construct a private wire under this subsection 1 of this section will require the 
licence holder to comply with technical standards that shall be set out by the Commission 
including those which may be necessary to ensure that private wires are compatible with the 
transmission or distribution system, to such extent as the Commission may specify in the 
licence. 
7. Private wires are exempt from the deﬁnition of transmission and distribution and therefore 
holders of a private wires licence or permission are exempt from the obligations of 
transmission system operator and distribution system operator.  
8. The Commission may for the purposes of making a levy order in under Schedule 1 paragraph 
16(a), designate private wires as a class of electricity undertaking.  
9. In assessing licence applications under subsection 1 and permission applications under 
subsection 2, the Commission may consult with the Board and EirGrid for the purposes of: 
a. Determining whether the licence is compliant with paragraphs (b) and (c) of 
subsection 3 of this section.

9 
 
b. Incorporating private wires into any electricity system mapping including 
programmes such as Dial Before You Dig.  
10. A licence holder to construct a private wire shall not be granted any wayleave or compulsory 
purchase order rights.  
11. The Commission may grant the Board a limited ‘step in’ right to take charge of a private wire 
for the purpose of asset decommissioning and removal in the interest of public safety where 
the original private wire licence holder is unable to decommission or remove the wire.  
12. The Commission may, on application of the Board, grant the Board a limited ‘step in’ right to 
take ownership of a private wire where it is viewed that the maintenance and operation of 
the wire by the Board would be beneﬁcial to the operation and development of the national 
grid.   
 
Explanatory Note: 
There are three categories of private wires to be regulated, for which provisions are provided for in 
this section: 
A) licence holders 
This includes private wires to be regulated under use case 1 of the policy statement. These are private 
wires which will be licenced under Head 6 and as such will be subject to a licence fee and tariﬀs. All 
licenced private wires must be built to the same electrical, technical and safety standards as the 
national grid (subsections 5 and 6). 
B) permission holders 
This includes private wires to be regulated under use case 2 and use case 4 of the policy statement 
which require comparatively less regulatory oversight as the works are much more limited. These cases 
should be assessed for a private wire permission under subsection 2. While private wire permissions 
will be required to be built to the same safety standards as the national grid (subsection 5), they 
constitute less extensive works so more lenient conditions may be applied to the technical standards.  
C) authorisations under local authorities 
In the case of EV charging, it is more appropriate for the private wire developer to apply directly to the 
relevant local authority for a road opening licence as mechanisms such as the Kerbo solution may 
require transport over third party lands and digging into footpaths. The CRU and ESB Networks should 
be notiﬁed of any works to centralise information of where electrical cables are laid in part to facilitate 
the Dial Before You Dig programme currently managed by ESB Networks (subsection 9). Therefore, 
local authorities will be required to provide ESB Networks with locations of on street EV charging, as 
well as provide the CRU with an annual report on the uptake of on street charging.  
Subsection 4 is to ensure that that the national grid is protected as private wires in some cases may 
require extensive works. Planned development and reinforcement of the grid (Subsection 4 (c)) refers 
to development committed to in the agreed upon Price Reviews. Furthermore, it is important that the 
acceleration of the deployment of renewable, sustainable and alternative forms of energy – as deﬁned 
in the 1999 Act – is highlighted, while also taking into considerations regarding security of supply as 
consistent with the guiding principles of the policy statement, other government policy including 
industrial policy, and the national climate objective.

10 
 
These private wires must also be strictly regulated by technical and safety standards (subsection 5 and 
6) – ideally those already in place by ESB Networks – and be capable of being subsumed by ESB 
Networks in the case of project decommissioning, bankruptcy of the private wire developer or other 
such event (subsection 11 and 12). 
Subsection 7 is to ensure that there are no obligations of private wires licence holders to comply with 
TSO and DSO requirements under EU law, such as unbundling of supply and generation.  
Subsection 8 is intended to provide clarity to the CRU that private wires can have distinct charging 
methodology applied under the Levy Order of Schedule I of the 1999 Act.  
Subsection 9 is to ensure the current TSO and DSO (EirGrid and ESB Networks respectively) are 
appropriately consulted in future private wire installations to limit negative impacts on the 
development of the national grid. This is also to ensure that private wires can be captured under 
national mapping programs such as Dial Before You Dig which enhances public safety.  
Subsection 10 is to prohibit private wires operators from receiving statutory wayleave and CPO rights 
as stated in the policy statement. 
Subsection 11 is to provide for a limited step in right for ESB Networks if a private wire needs to be 
decommissioned and removed in the interest of public safety where the original company is unable to 
provide this service such as in the case of company bankruptcy, wire abandonment or other issue of 
last resort.  
Subsection 12 is to provide a limited step in right for ESB Networks, allowing ESB Networks to take over 
as owner and operator of a private wires where the wire is deemed by both the system operators and 
the CRU to be beneﬁcial to the build out of the national grid. This right will only be enforced where 
there is consent from the CRU, ESB Networks and EirGrid and may be completed at distribution or 
transmission level. Any transfer of ownership may be subject to compensation as agreed between the 
system operator and the private wire operator.

11 
 
Head 8 – Provision to ensure the reviewing of private wires legislation 
To provide that the following provision is inserted:  
The Minister shall, having consulted with the Commission, not later than ten years after this Act 
comes into force, carry out a review thereof. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
The policy statement and associated Government decision from which this General Scheme has arisen 
makes a commitment to “continue to monitor industry developments e.g. the emerging concept of 
green energy parks to identify any future need for further liberalisation [of the legislation].” This initial 
legislated reform in this Scheme is intended to allow for four unique circumstances of private wires, as 
elucidated in the policy statement, but recognises that there may be further circumstances under 
which private wires could be build that would aid in the achievement of Ireland’s renewable energy 
and decarbonisation targets. For example, exploring a more ﬂexible legislative regime for green energy 
industrial parks or renewable energy communities.  
Due to this evolving nature of the electricity grid, it would be ideal to have a review mechanism built 
into the legislation to allow for revision at least every 10 years, or earlier should the need arise. This 
review power should be conferred on the Minister of Climate, Energy and the Environment as the 
authority over energy policy and the ERA; however, the Minister should be required to consult with 
the CRU who will likely be responsible for overseeing and implementing any regulatory reform.

12 
 
Head 9 – A safety regime for Internal Collector Cable Systems 
To provide that Section 9C of the 1999 Act, is amended by the insertion of a Section 9CB: 
Where: 
(a) The Commission shall make regulations relating to electrical safety and technical standards 
of internal collector cable systems. 
(b) The Commission shall consult the Board and EirGrid in preparation of regulations to ensure 
internal collector cable systems are functionally compliant with the electrical, technical and 
safety standards of the national grid. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
Wind and solar farms often have extensive networks of cables to collect generated electricity from 
individual wind turbines or solar panels and bring them to a central point where the farm connects to 
the national grid. These wires can be lengthy, and in some cases cross roads and third party owned 
land. However, there are no publicly adopted standards or mechanisms to inspect such internal 
collector cable systems. 
Under the policy statement, the CRU should be given powers to adopt technical and safety standards 
for the design and safe operation for these systems, heretofore known as internal collector cable 
systems. These standards may be diﬀerent than those required for private wires as internal collector 
cable systems often operate at lower voltages. As such, the safety and technical standards for internal 
collector cable systems should be developed separately to the private wires safety regime proposed 
under Head 5.

13 
 
Head 10 – Commencement Date for Head 9 
To provide that the provision under Head 9 shall come into eﬀect at a later date than the rest of the 
Bill. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
The intention of this Head is to allow for the private wires regime to be set up in the ﬁrst instance 
following the enaction of the Bill. It is intended that the regime for internal collector cable systems will 
follow this.

14 
 
Head 11 – Funding of CRU in the development of a Private Wires regime 
To provide that the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment may provide such assistance, 
including ﬁnancial assistance to the Commission as the Minister consider appropriate in relation to the 
development of a Private Wires regime. 
Any assistance provided by the Minister shall be subject to conditions, if any, determined by the 
Minister. 
 
Explanatory Note: 
The Commission are funded through levy orders placed on energy undertakings that they regulate. 
The regulator will be unable to receive funding for the private wires function until there are 
participants in the regime. This provision will provide for the ability of the Minister to provide ﬁnancial 
assistance to the CRU to develop this regime.
